faq.q: How does a dome stay up?
faq.a: A dome works like many arches rotated around a centre. Its curved shell carries weight down to the supporting walls in compression, so it can span a big space with nothing in the middle.

faq.q: Why is the top of a dome in compression?
faq.a: The shell's weight presses down the curve, and near the crown it also squeezes the horizontal rings of the dome together, so the whole upper part is squashed. Masonry and concrete are strong when squashed.
asks: What forces are in a dome?

faq.q: Why do domes push outward at the base?
faq.a: Lower down, the shell tends to spread outward around its rim, which is called hoop tension. Masonry is weak in tension, so old domes often cracked there.
asks: Why do domes crack at the bottom?

faq.q: What holds the base of a dome together?
faq.a: Builders use a ring that works in tension: iron chains, stone or timber rings, or steel bands, helped by thick walls and buttresses. The dome of St Peter's Basilica in Rome is bound with iron chains.

faq.q: How did the Romans build the Pantheon dome?
faq.a: They used concrete, heavy at the bottom and mixed with light volcanic stone near the top, and made the dome thinner as it rose. The open oculus at the crown removes the heaviest part.
asks: Why does the Pantheon have a hole in the roof?

facts: The Pantheon in Rome, completed around 125 CE, has a dome 43.3 metres across, still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
A dome's lower part is stretched around its rim by hoop tension, while its upper part is squeezed.
